stem: Lena tracked her typing speed each week. Which scatter plot matches her data?

choices.why: Each dot is one row of the table, like (1, 26) and (6, 36).
This plot switched the axes. Weeks should go on the x-axis and speed on the y-axis.
This plot matched the weeks with the speeds in reverse order. Week 1 goes with 26, not 36.
Two points are mixed up. Week 3 should be 29 and Week 4 should be 32.

hint: Turn each row into a point (week, speed) and find it on each graph.
explain: Weeks of practice goes on the x-axis. Typing speed goes on the y-axis.
The correct plot shows these six dots rising from left to right.

stem: A snack stand recorded the temperature and the cups of hot cocoa sold each day. What kind of association does the scatter plot show?

choices.t: Negative: as temperature goes up, cocoa sales go down.
choices.why: The dots fall from left to right, so the association is negative.

choices.t: Positive: as temperature goes up, cocoa sales go down.
choices.why: The description is right, but that pattern is called negative, not positive.

choices.t: Positive: as temperature goes up, cocoa sales go up.
choices.why: Look again. The dots on the right (hot days) are lower, not higher.

choices.t: No association: the points are not exactly on a line.
choices.why: Points do not need to be on a line. There is still a clear downward trend.

hint: Read the dots from left to right. Do they go up or down?
explain: Start at the left (cold days): about 52 cups sold.
Move right (hot days): sales drop to 15 cups.
When x goes up and y goes down, the association is negative.

stem: A scientist counts bacteria in a dish every hour. Is the association between time and number of bacteria linear or non-linear?

choices.t: Non-linear: the change grows each hour, so the points curve.
choices.why: The jumps are +1, +2, +4, +8, … so the rate is not constant and the points bend.

choices.t: Linear: the number of bacteria always goes up.
choices.why: Always going up does not make it linear. The points must go up by the same amount each time.

choices.t: Linear: the bacteria go up by the same amount each hour.
choices.why: Check the jumps: +1, +2, +4, +8, +16, +32. They are not the same.

choices.t: Non-linear: the number of bacteria goes down over time.
choices.why: Look again. The number of bacteria goes up, from 1 to 64.

hint: Find how much the number of bacteria changes each hour. Is it the same each time?
explain: Changes each hour: +1, +2, +4, +8, +16, +32.
The change is not the same, so the rate of change is not constant.
The points curve upward, so the association is non-linear.

stem: The scatter plot shows hours worked in one week and weekly pay for 9 teens. Which statement describes the clusters and the outlier?

choices.t: Two clusters (4–6 hours and 18–21 hours); outlier (20, 90)
choices.why: Most teens earn about $10 an hour, but (20, 90) earned far less than others who worked 20 hours.

choices.t: Two clusters (4–6 hours and 18–21 hours); outlier (4, 40)
choices.why: (4, 40) is the lowest point, but it fits the pattern. An outlier is far from the pattern, not just the smallest.

choices.t: One cluster (all 9 teens); outlier (21, 210)
choices.why: (21, 210) is the highest point, but it fits the pattern. Also, the points form two separate groups.

choices.t: Two clusters (4–6 hours and 18–21 hours); no outlier
choices.why: (20, 90) is far below the other points near 20 hours, so it is an outlier.

hint: Look for groups of dots that are close together, then look for one dot that does not fit the pattern.
explain: One group worked 4–6 hours and earned $40–$60. Another group worked 18–21 hours and earned $180–$210.
The pattern is about $10 per hour, so 20 hours should pay about $200.
(20, 90) is far below that, so it is the outlier.

stem: Eight students measured their height and their arm span. Which statement best describes the strength of the association?

choices.t: Strong positive: the points stay very close to an upward line.
choices.why: Every arm span is within about 1 inch of the line, so the association is strong.

choices.t: Weak positive: the points are not all exactly on one line.
choices.why: Points do not need to be exactly on a line to be strong. These are very close to it.

choices.t: Strong negative: the points are very close to a line.
choices.why: They are close to a line, but the line goes up from left to right, so it is positive.

choices.t: Strong positive: the numbers are all large (over 55 in.).
choices.why: Big numbers do not show strength. Strength is about how close the points are to a line.

hint: Picture a line through the dots. Are the dots close to it or spread out?
explain: As height goes up, arm span goes up, so the association is positive.
Each arm span is within about 1 inch of the student's height, so the dots hug a line.
Dots that stay very close to a line show a strong association.

stem: Students recorded how far they live from school and how long it takes to get there. Which statement identifies the outlier and explains how it differs from the pattern?

choices.t: (3, 35): the trip takes far longer than the pattern predicts for 3 miles.
choices.why: That point is about 24 minutes above the pattern of about 3 minutes per mile.

choices.t: (6, 20): it is the farthest distance from school, so it does not fit.
choices.why: (6, 20) is at the end of the data, but it follows the pattern of 3 minutes per mile.

choices.t: (1, 5): it is the closest to school, so it is far from the other points.
choices.why: (1, 5) is at the start of the pattern. Being first does not make it an outlier.

choices.t: (3, 35): that student lives much farther from school than the others.
choices.why: Right point, wrong reason. The student lives 3 miles away, like another student. The time is what is unusual.

hint: Find the pattern first. How many minutes does each extra mile add?
explain: Pattern: travel time goes up about 3 minutes for each mile (5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20).
Another student who lives 3 miles away takes 11 minutes.
(3, 35) is 35 − 11 = 24 minutes above the pattern, so it is the outlier.

stem: A café recorded the daily high temperature, cups of lemonade sold, and bowls of soup sold for 8 days. How do the two associations differ?

choices.t: Lemonade: strong positive. Soup: weak negative.
choices.why: Lemonade dots hug an upward line. Soup dots trend down but zigzag a lot.

choices.t: Lemonade: strong positive. Soup: strong negative.
choices.why: Soup does trend down, but the dots jump up and down a lot, so it is weak.

choices.t: Lemonade: weak positive. Soup: strong negative.
choices.why: You switched the strengths. The lemonade dots are the ones that stay close to a line.

choices.t: Lemonade: strong negative. Soup: weak positive.
choices.why: You switched the directions. Lemonade goes up as it gets hotter, and soup goes down.

hint: For each plot, ask two questions: Do the dots go up or down? Are they close to a line or spread out?
explain: Lemonade rises about 5 cups for every 5°F, and the dots stay close to a line: strong positive.
Soup tends to drop (34 at 50°F, 20 at 85°F), so it is negative.
But soup sales zigzag (34, 24, 36, 23, …), so the dots are spread out: weak.
The plots differ in strength and in direction.

stem: A health class asked 10 students about screen time after 8 p.m. and hours of sleep that night. Which analysis of the scatter plot is correct?

choices.t: Negative; clusters at 1–2 h and 5–6 h; outlier (1.5, 5). More screen time tends to go with less sleep, but this does not prove it causes it.
choices.why: This describes the direction, both clusters, the outlier, and avoids claiming cause.

choices.t: Negative; clusters at 1–2 h and 5–6 h; outlier (1.5, 5). This proves that screen time after 8 p.m. causes students to sleep less.
choices.why: A scatter plot shows an association. It cannot prove that one thing causes the other.

choices.t: Positive; clusters at 1–2 h and 5–6 h; outlier (1.5, 5). More screen time tends to go with more sleep, but this does not prove it causes it.
choices.why: The dots fall from left to right, so the association is negative, not positive.

choices.t: Negative; clusters at 1–2 h and 5–6 h; outlier (6, 6). More screen time tends to go with less sleep, but this does not prove it causes it.
choices.why: (6, 6) fits the pattern. The outlier is (1.5, 5): little screen time but very little sleep.

hint: Check four things: direction, clusters, the point that does not fit, and whether a plot can prove cause.
explain: As screen time goes up, sleep goes down, so the association is negative.
One cluster is at 1–2 hours of screen time (8.5–9.5 h sleep). Another is at 5–6 hours (6–7 h sleep).
(1.5, 5) had little screen time but very little sleep, so it is the outlier.
The pattern suggests more late screen time goes with less sleep, but it does not prove cause.

stem: Ava says a graph of a person's height from birth to age 30 would be linear. Which argument about Ava's claim is correct?

choices.t: Ava is wrong. Babies grow fast, then growth slows, and it stops in the late teens, so the rate of change is not constant.
choices.why: Height grows at a changing rate and then levels off, so the graph curves.

choices.t: Ava is right. Height goes up every year from birth to 30, so the graph is a straight line.
choices.why: Going up is not enough for linear. Also, adults stop growing, so height does not go up every year.

choices.t: Ava is right. A person grows about the same amount every year until age 30.
choices.why: People grow much more as babies than as teens, and most stop growing in their late teens.

choices.t: Ava is wrong. Height goes down as people get older, so the graph falls.
choices.why: From birth to 30, height goes up and then levels off. It does not fall.

hint: Think about how fast a baby grows compared to a teen and an adult.
explain: A linear graph needs a constant rate of change.
Babies grow very fast, older kids grow more slowly, and growth stops in the late teens.
The rate of change is not constant, so the graph curves up and then levels off: non-linear.

stem: The table shows minutes of bike riding and calories burned. Which graph shows the most reasonable line of best fit?

choices.why: This line follows the trend with about half the points above it and half below.
This line is too steep. By the end, every point is below it.
This line is flat, but the calories go up. The line must go up too.
This line has a good slope, but it sits above all the points. It should go through the middle.

hint: A good line of best fit goes the same direction as the dots and has dots on both sides.
explain: The dots go up from left to right, so the line must go up.
The best line runs through the middle of the dots.
For y = 9x, 4 points are a little above and 4 are a little below (within 10 calories).

stem: Jordan drew the line y = 3x + 2 for this car-wash data. He says, “This can't be a line of best fit because it only goes through 2 of the 6 points.” Which response is correct?

choices.t: Jordan is wrong. A line of best fit shows the trend; points can be above and below it.
choices.why: The other points are only 1 car above or below the line, so it is a good fit.

choices.t: Jordan is right. A line of best fit must pass through every point.
choices.why: A line of best fit summarizes the trend. It is not supposed to connect the dots.

choices.t: Jordan is right. A line of best fit must pass through at least half the points.
choices.why: There is no rule like this. A line can be a great fit and touch no points at all.

choices.t: Jordan is wrong. A line of best fit only has to go through the first and last points.
choices.why: The line should run through the middle of all the points, not just the ends.

hint: Is a line of best fit supposed to connect the dots, or show the overall trend?
explain: The line passes through (2, 8) and (5, 17).
The other 4 points are just 1 car away: 2 above the line and 2 below.
A line of best fit shows the overall trend with points balanced around it, so Jordan is wrong.

stem: Two students drew lines for data about rows a gardener planted and hours of work. Line A is y = x + 1.5. Line B is y = 1.5x − 1. Which line fits the data better?

choices.t: Line A, because every point is close to it, with some above and some below.
choices.why: Every point is within 0.5 hour of Line A, so it fits best.

choices.t: Line B, because it goes through more of the points.
choices.why: Line B touches (4, 5) and (6, 8), but then it moves far above the other points.

choices.t: Line B, because it is steeper, so it shows the growth better.
choices.why: Steeper is not better. Line B rises faster than the data, so it ends far above the points.

choices.t: Line A, because it starts higher on the y-axis.
choices.why: Line A is the better fit, but not because of where it starts. Look at how close the points are.

hint: For each line, check how far the points on the right side are from it.
explain: Line A at x = 16 gives 17.5. The actual value is 18, only 0.5 away.
Line B at x = 16 gives 23. That is 5 away from 18.
Every point is within 0.5 of Line A, and the points are on both sides of it.
Closer points mean a better fit, so Line A fits better.

stem: A class measured a sunflower each week. The line of best fit passes through (2, 34) and (8, 52). What is the slope of the line?

choices.t: 3 cm per week
{{1|3}} cm per week
choices.why: You divided change in x by change in y. Slope is change in y ÷ change in x.

choices.t: 18 cm per week
choices.why: 18 cm is the total change over 6 weeks. Divide by 6 to get the change per week.

choices.t: 6.5 cm per week
choices.why: You divided 52 by 8. Use the change in y and the change in x between the two points.

hint: Slope = change in height ÷ change in weeks between the two points.
explain: Change in y: 52 − 34 = 18 cm.
Change in x: 8 − 2 = 6 weeks.
Slope = 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so the sunflower grows about 3 cm per week.

stem: A coach tracked push-ups in one minute after each week of training. A line of best fit goes through (1, 22) and (6, 42). What is the equation of the line?

choices.why: 22 is the y-value at x = 1, not at x = 0. Solve 22 = 4(1) + b to find b.
You added 4 instead of subtracting. 22 = 4 + b, so b = 22 − 4.
This line goes through (1, 22) but not (6, 42): 5(6) + 17 = 47. Slope = 20 ÷ 5 = 4.

hint: Find the slope first, then put one point into y = mx + b to find b.

stem: The plot shows daily players (in thousands) of a phone game. In Week 8 the game had a big update. Sam drew the line y = −x + 26 using all 8 points. How well does Sam's line model the data?

choices.t: Not well. The Week 8 outlier pulled the right end up, so the line is too flat.
choices.why: Weeks 1–7 drop about 2.5 thousand a week, but Sam's line drops only 1 thousand a week.

choices.t: Well. About half the points are above the line and half are below it.
choices.why: Counting is not enough. Weeks 1–3 are on or above the line and Weeks 4–7 are below it, so it misses the trend.

choices.t: Not well. The Week 8 outlier pulled the line down, so it is too steep.
choices.why: The outlier is high, so it pulls the line up. That makes the line flatter, not steeper.

choices.t: Well. The line should follow Week 8 because it is the newest data.
choices.why: Week 8 is an outlier from the update. It does not follow the pattern of Weeks 1–7.

hint: Look at Weeks 1–7 only. Are they balanced around Sam's line, or above at the start and below at the end?
explain: Weeks 1–7 drop about 2.5 thousand players each week in a steady line.
Weeks 1–2 are above Sam's line, and Weeks 4–7 are below it (Week 7: the line says 19, actual 13).
The Week 8 point (30) is far above the trend, so it pulls the right end of the line up and makes it too flat.
A line like y = −2.5x + 30.3 fits Weeks 1–7 much better.

stem: A class tracked the total books read after each week of a reading challenge. Line A is y = 3x + 9. Line B is y = 4x + 6. Which argument is correct?

choices.t: Line A is better: the points stay within 1 book of it, with some above and some below.
choices.why: Line A stays close to every point. Line B ends 4–5 books above the last points.

choices.t: Line B is better: it is steeper, so it shows the books going up faster.
choices.why: The data rise about 3 books a week. A slope of 4 is too steep, so Line B pulls away from the points.

choices.t: Line B is better: it is above most of the points, so it covers all the data.
choices.why: A good line goes through the middle of the points, not above them.

choices.t: Line A is better: it goes through every one of the points.
choices.why: Line A is better, but it only goes through 1 point (Week 2). It is better because the others are close to it.

hint: Check the last few weeks. How far is each line from the points there?
explain: Line A: every point is 0 or 1 book away, with points on both sides.
Line B: at Week 8 it gives 4(8) + 6 = 38, but the actual total is 34 (4 away).
The data rise about 3 books per week, so a slope of 4 is too steep.
Line A stays close all the way across, so it is the better model.

stem: Two classes recorded hours studied and scores on a 100-point test. For both classes, the line of best fit is y = 5x + 60. Which statement is correct?

choices.t: It models Class A better, since its points are closer to the line. A limit: at 9 hours it predicts 105, which is not possible.
choices.why: Closer points mean a stronger model, and scores cannot go above 100.

choices.t: It models Class B better, since its points are more spread out. A limit: at 9 hours it predicts 105, which is not possible.
choices.why: Spread-out points mean a weaker model. The closer the points, the better the line fits.

choices.t: It models both classes the same, since it is the same line. A limit: at 9 hours it predicts 105, which is not possible.
choices.why: The same line can fit one set of points well and another poorly. Look at the distances.

choices.t: It models Class A better, since its points are closer to the line. It has no limit, so it works for any number of hours.
choices.why: Every model has limits. At 9 hours this one predicts 105, but scores stop at 100.

hint: Compare how far the points are from the line in each graph. Then try a large number of hours in the equation.
explain: Class A scores are all within 1 point of the line: a strong linear model.
Class B scores are 5 to 14 points away: a weak model, so its predictions are less reliable.
Limit: at 9 hours, 5(9) + 60 = 105, but a test score cannot go above 100.

stem: The model y = −8x + 100 shows a tablet's battery while streaming video. x is hours of video and y is battery percent. What does the slope mean?

choices.t: The battery goes down 8 percentage points each hour.
choices.why: The slope is −8: the battery drops 8 points per hour.

choices.t: The battery goes up 8 percentage points each hour.
choices.why: The slope is negative, so the battery goes down, not up.

choices.t: The battery starts at 8 percent when video begins.
choices.why: The starting value is the y-intercept, 100 percent, not the slope.

choices.t: The battery lasts for 8 hours of streaming video.
choices.why: The battery lasts 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5 hours. The 8 is how much it drops each hour.

hint: In y = mx + b, the slope m tells how much y changes each time x goes up by 1.
explain: In y = mx + b, the slope is m = −8.
Slope is the rate of change: battery percent per hour of video.
Negative means it goes down, so the battery drops 8 percentage points each hour.

stem: Malik's savings are modeled by y = 15x + 40. x is the number of weeks and y is the dollars in his account. What does the y-intercept mean?

choices.t: Malik had $40 in his account at the start.
choices.why: The y-intercept is the value of y when x = 0, so he started with $40.

choices.t: Malik adds $40 to his account each week.
choices.why: He adds $15 each week. That is the slope, not the y-intercept.

choices.t: Malik had $15 in his account at the start.
choices.why: 15 is the slope (dollars per week). The y-intercept is the b in y = mx + b.

choices.t: Malik has $40 in his account after 1 week.
choices.why: After 1 week he has 15(1) + 40 = $55. The y-intercept is at 0 weeks.

hint: The y-intercept is where x = 0. What does x = 0 mean here?
explain: In y = mx + b, the y-intercept is b = 40.
The y-intercept is the value of y when x = 0 weeks.
So at the start, before any weeks of saving, Malik had $40.

stem: The height of a young oak tree is modeled by y = 0.5x + 3. x is the age in years and y is the height in feet. Predict the tree's height at 12 years.

choices.t: 9 feet
6 feet
choices.why: 6 is 0.5 × 12. You still need to add the starting height of 3 feet.

choices.t: 7.5 feet
choices.why: You added 12 + 3 first. Multiply 0.5 × 12 first, then add 3.

choices.t: 15 feet
choices.why: You added 12 + 3 and skipped the 0.5. Multiply 12 by 0.5 first.

hint: Put 12 in for x, multiply, then add.
explain: Substitute x = 12: y = 0.5(12) + 3.
Multiply: 0.5 × 12 = 6.
Add: 6 + 3 = 9 feet.

stem: A gym charges a $25 sign-up fee plus $30 per month. Which linear model and answer are correct for how many months it takes for the total cost to reach $295?

choices.t: y = 30x + 25; 9 months
y = 25x + 30; 10.6 months
choices.why: The $30 per month is the rate (slope), and the $25 fee is the start (y-intercept). You switched them.

choices.t: y = 30x + 25; about 10.7 months
choices.why: You added 25 instead of subtracting it. Subtract the fee: 295 − 25 = 270.

choices.t: y = 55x; about 5.4 months
choices.why: The $25 fee is paid only once. It is not added every month.

hint: The one-time fee is the starting value. The monthly charge is the rate of change.
explain: Rate of change: $30 per month. Starting value: $25. Model: y = 30x + 25.
Subtract 25: 30x = 270. Divide by 30: x = 9 months.
Trend: the total cost goes up $30 every month.

stem: A candle's height is modeled by y = −1.5x + 24. x is hours burning and y is height in centimeters. Which statement is true?

choices.t: It starts 24 cm tall and burns out after 16 hours.
choices.why: Burned out means y = 0: 1.5x = 24, so x = 16.

choices.t: It starts 24 cm tall and burns out after 24 hours.
choices.why: That would be true only if it lost 1 cm per hour. It loses 1.5 cm per hour: 24 ÷ 1.5 = 16.

choices.t: It starts 1.5 cm tall and grows 24 cm each hour.
choices.why: You switched the slope and y-intercept. The 24 is the start and −1.5 is the change per hour.

choices.t: It starts 24 cm tall and is 33 cm tall after 6 hours.
choices.why: The slope is negative, so the candle gets shorter: 24 − 9 = 15 cm after 6 hours.

hint: The y-intercept is the starting height. Burned out means the height is 0.
explain: y-intercept = 24: the candle is 24 cm tall before it is lit.
Slope = −1.5: it gets 1.5 cm shorter each hour.
After 6 hours: −1.5(6) + 24 = 15 cm.
Burned out: −1.5x + 24 = 0, so 1.5x = 24 and x = 16 hours.

stem: A bake sale's line of best fit is y = mx + 15. x is hours the sale is open and y is total dollars earned. The line passes through (4, 75). How many hours must the sale be open to earn $165?

choices.t: 10 hours
11 hours
choices.why: 165 ÷ 15 = 11 skips the starting $15. Subtract 15 first: 150 ÷ 15 = 10.

choices.t: 8 hours
choices.why: You used m = 75 ÷ 4. Subtract the 15 first: 75 − 15 = 60, and 60 ÷ 4 = 15.

choices.t: 12 hours
choices.why: You added 15 instead of subtracting it. 15x = 165 − 15 = 150.

hint: First use the point (4, 75) to find m. Then set y = 165.
explain: Subtract 15: 60 = 4m, so m = 15.
Subtract 15: 15x = 150, so x = 10 hours.

stem: Students counted cricket chirps per minute at different temperatures. A line of best fit passes through (60, 80) and (80, 160). Which equation and prediction for 72°F are correct?

choices.t: y = 4x − 160; about 128 chirps
y = 4x + 80; about 368 chirps
choices.why: 80 is the y-value at x = 60, not at x = 0. Solve 80 = 4(60) + b to find b.

choices.t: y = {{1|4}}x + 65; about 83 chirps
choices.why: You divided change in x by change in y. Slope = 80 ÷ 20 = 4.

choices.t: y = 4x − 160; about 448 chirps
choices.why: The equation is right, but you added 160. 288 − 160 = 128.

hint: Find the slope, then use one point to find b. Then put in x = 72.
explain: Slope: (160 − 80) ÷ (80 − 60) = 80 ÷ 20 = 4, so about 4 more chirps per minute for each 1°F.
Equation: y = 4x − 160.
At 72°F: 4(72) − 160 = 288 − 160 = 128 chirps per minute.

stem: The plot shows a child's height each year. A line of best fit passes through (2, 34) and (10, 54). Which model and evaluation are correct?

choices.t: y = 2.5x + 29. Age 12: about 59 in. (reasonable). Age 30: about 104 in. (not reasonable).
choices.why: Age 12 is close to the data, but people stop growing in their teens, so 104 in. is too tall.

choices.t: y = 2.5x + 29. Age 12: about 59 in. (reasonable). Age 30: about 104 in. (reasonable).
choices.why: 104 in. is over 8 feet tall. The trend does not continue, because people stop growing.

choices.t: y = 2.5x + 34. Age 12: about 64 in. (reasonable). Age 30: about 109 in. (not reasonable).
choices.why: 34 is the height at age 2, not at age 0. Solve 34 = 2.5(2) + b to get b = 29.

choices.t: y = 2.5x + 29. Age 12: about 59 in. (not reasonable). Age 30: about 104 in. (not reasonable).
choices.why: Age 12 is just 2 years past the data, and 59 in. (4 ft 11 in.) is a normal height.

hint: Find the model, then ask: does each prediction make sense for a real person?
explain: Age 12: 2.5(12) + 29 = 59 in., close to the data, so it is reasonable.
Age 30: 2.5(30) + 29 = 104 in. (8 ft 8 in.), which is not realistic.
Predicting far beyond the data (extrapolation) can be unreliable.

stem: A librarian asked 90 students if they prefer books on paper or on a screen. 50 were 7th graders and the rest were 8th graders. 30 of the 7th graders prefer paper. 18 of the 8th graders prefer a screen. Which two-way table is correct?

choices.why: All the counts match the story and the grand total is 90.
The 8th grade total should be 90 − 50 = 40, not 50. So 8th grade paper is 40 − 18 = 22.
The 18 belongs in the 8th grade Screen box, not the Paper box.
You switched the 7th grade boxes. 30 of the 7th graders prefer paper, so 30 goes under Paper.

hint: Start with the grand total of 90, then find the 8th grade total.
explain: 8th grade total = 90 − 50 = 40.
7th grade screen = 50 − 30 = 20. 8th grade paper = 40 − 18 = 22.
Column totals: paper = 30 + 22 = 52; screen = 20 + 18 = 38.

stem: A school surveyed students about eating breakfast. How many 7th graders skip breakfast, and what kind of frequency is it?

choices.t: 25; a joint frequency
choices.why: 25 is where the 7th grade row and the Skips column meet, so it is a joint frequency.

choices.t: 25; a marginal frequency
choices.why: 25 is the right count, but it is inside the table. Marginal frequencies are the totals on the edges.

choices.t: 75; a marginal frequency
choices.why: 75 is all students who skip breakfast. The question asks about 7th graders only.

choices.t: 60; a marginal frequency
choices.why: 60 is the total number of 7th graders, including those who eat breakfast.

hint: Find where the 7th grade row and the Skips breakfast column cross.
explain: Go across the 7th grade row to the Skips breakfast column: 25.
This count is inside the table, for one row and one column, so it is a joint frequency.
Totals on the edges (like 75 or 60) are marginal frequencies.

stem: A movie theater asked 125 customers which snack they bought. What is the relative frequency of customers who bought candy?

choices.why: 48 is the count of customers. Divide it by the total, 125.
22 ÷ 125 counts only kids. Adults who bought candy count too: 22 + 26 = 48.

choices.t: About 62.3%
choices.why: You divided by 77, the popcorn total. Divide by all 125 customers.

hint: Relative frequency = count ÷ total. Find the candy total first.
explain: Customers who bought candy: 22 + 26 = 48.
Total customers: 125.

stem: Students were asked how far they live from school and whether they bike to school. What percent of students who live more than 2 miles away bike to school?

choices.t: About 21.1%
choices.why: You divided by 57, the bike total. The question is about the students who live more than 2 miles away (80).

choices.t: About 9.2%
choices.why: You divided by 130, all students. Use only the “more than 2 miles” row total.
68 ÷ 80 is the percent who do not bike. The question asks who bikes.

hint: “Of students who live more than 2 miles away” tells you which total to divide by.
explain: Use the “more than 2 miles” row. Its total is 80.
In that row, 12 students bike.

stem: A survey asked teens whether they have a weeknight curfew and whether they usually get 8 or more hours of sleep. Which statement correctly uses relative frequencies?

choices.t: Association: 70% with a curfew get 8+ hours, but only 40% without one do.
choices.why: 42 ÷ 60 = 70% and 30 ÷ 75 = 40%. Those are far apart, so there seems to be an association.

choices.t: No association: 72 teens get 8+ hours and 63 do not, which is about the same.
choices.why: Those are column totals. Compare the percent in each row instead.

choices.t: No association: 70% with a curfew and 60% without one get 8+ hours.
choices.why: 45 ÷ 75 = 60% is the no-curfew teens who get less than 8 hours. Use 30 ÷ 75 = 40%.

choices.t: Association: 42 ÷ 135 ≈ 31% of all teens have a curfew and get 8+ hours.
choices.why: Dividing by the grand total does not compare the two groups. Divide each row by its own total.

hint: Find the percent who get 8+ hours in each row, using that row's total.
explain: Curfew: 42 ÷ 60 = 0.70 = 70% get 8+ hours.
No curfew: 30 ÷ 75 = 0.40 = 40% get 8+ hours.
The percents are 30 points apart, so teens with a curfew are more likely to get 8+ hours.
This shows an association, not proof that a curfew causes more sleep.

stem: A store recorded how 200 shoppers paid. Maria calculated 12 ÷ 80 = 0.15. What does 0.15 mean here?

choices.t: 15% of shoppers under 25 paid cash.
choices.why: Maria divided by 80, the Under 25 total, so her result is about shoppers under 25.

choices.t: 15% of all shoppers were under 25 and paid cash.
choices.why: For all shoppers, divide by 200: 12 ÷ 200 = 6%.

choices.t: 15% of shoppers who paid cash were under 25.
choices.why: For cash shoppers, divide by the cash total: 12 ÷ 60 = 20%.

choices.t: 15% of shoppers under 25 paid by card.
choices.why: 12 is in the Paid cash column. Under 25 shoppers who paid by card: 68 ÷ 80 = 85%.

hint: Look at the number Maria divided by. Which group has a total of 80?
explain: 12 is the number of shoppers who are under 25 and paid cash.
80 is the total of the Under 25 row.
So 12 ÷ 80 = 0.15 means 15% of shoppers under 25 paid cash.

stem: A teacher surveyed students about video games on school nights and homework. Kayla says, “More students in the second group turn homework in on time, but that's only because the groups are different sizes.” Which response is correct?

choices.t: Kayla is wrong: 48% of 2+ hour gamers are on time vs. 70% of the others, so there is an association.
choices.why: Percents fix the group-size problem, and 48% vs. 70% is a big gap.

choices.t: Kayla is right: the groups are different sizes, so they cannot be compared.
choices.why: Groups of different sizes can be compared with percents. That is why we use relative frequencies.

choices.t: Kayla is wrong: 56 is more than 36, so the counts prove there is an association.
choices.why: Raw counts can mislead when groups differ in size. Compare percents instead.

choices.t: Kayla is wrong: 48% vs. 70% proves that playing games causes late homework.
choices.why: The percents show an association, but a survey cannot prove that one thing causes the other.

hint: Turn each row into a percent so the different group sizes do not matter.
explain: Games 2+ hours: 36 ÷ 75 = 0.48 = 48% on time.
Games less than 2 hours: 56 ÷ 80 = 0.70 = 70% on time.
The percents differ by 22 points, so the difference is not just group size.
There is an association, but it does not prove gaming causes late work.

stem: A class surveyed students about which hand they write with and whether they prefer dogs or cats. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.t: No association: 62.5% of both groups prefer dogs, so handedness does not help predict pet choice.
choices.why: 40 ÷ 64 and 45 ÷ 72 are both 62.5%, so the variables appear unrelated.

choices.t: Association: more right-handed (45) than left-handed (40) students prefer dogs, so they are linked.
choices.why: Those are counts from groups of different sizes. As percents, both are 62.5%.

choices.t: Association: 85 students prefer dogs but only 51 prefer cats, so hand and pet are linked.
choices.why: That shows dogs are more popular overall. It does not compare left- and right-handed students.

choices.t: No association: there are about the same number of left- and right-handed students in the class.
choices.why: Group sizes do not tell you about an association. Compare the percent in each row.

hint: Find the percent of each row that prefers dogs. Are they close or far apart?
explain: Left-handed: 40 ÷ 64 = 0.625 = 62.5% prefer dogs.
Right-handed: 45 ÷ 72 = 0.625 = 62.5% prefer dogs.
The percents are the same, so there is no association.
Knowing someone's writing hand does not help predict whether they prefer dogs or cats.
